source.title: A Comparison of Lower Body Power Characteristics Between Collegiate Athletes from Different Competition Levels

paper.citation: Stahl CA, Lindsay KG, Mann JB, Hunt M, Dawes JJ. A Comparison of Lower Body Power Characteristics Between Collegiate Athletes from Different Competition Levels. International Journal of Exercise Science. 2020;13(6):470-479.
paper.abstract: This archival study of 275 countermovement jump (CMJ) records from routine testing at three US universities compared jump characteristics by sex and competition level in NCAA Division I (DI) and NAIA athletes. After 10 outliers were removed, 265 were analysed for jump height, peak power and concentric rate of power development over the first 100 ms (RPD-100ms). The aim was to describe how CMJ characteristics relate to competition level and to report descriptive values for each group.
paper.tldr: Sex and competition level were both associated with CMJ profiles, and the authors report a roughly 5 cm jump height gap between DI and NAIA females but only roughly 1 cm between DI and NAIA males. Pooling the sexes would hide that difference, and the group averages are a rough reference for similar groups tested the same way, not a standard for any individual athlete.
paper.methods: Archival CMJ records from routine testing included NCAA DI males and females from two universities and NAIA males and females from one university. Jumps were measured on dual single-axis force plates at 1000 Hz, with jump height calculated from flight time and the higher of two successful trials used. A 2 x 2 multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) for sex and competition level on the three outcomes was followed by separate ANOVAs and a discriminant function analysis.
paper.findings: Sex and competition level together were associated with the three CMJ variables (Wilks' lambda = 0.908, F(3,259) = 8.732, p < .001, partial eta-squared = .092). DI females had higher values than NAIA females on jump height (32.2 cm vs 27.4 cm), peak power (3264.3 W vs 2835.7 W) and concentric RPD-100ms (15548.7 W/s vs 11718.7 W/s), whereas DI males differed from NAIA males only in peak power (4888.6 W vs 4538.6 W). A single discriminant function separated the groups mainly on jump height (structure coefficient .861) and peak power (.821), and both female groups differed from both male groups on the discriminant scores.
paper.limitations: Box's M was violated (p < .001), which the authors say reduces the trustworthiness of the MANOVA, and neither body mass nor sport was used as a covariate. The data are archival routine testing, the sample is two DI universities and one NAIA university with mean ages of 19.4 to 19.5 years, and the text gives no reliability data for these measures in this sample. Several reported values conflict: the NAIA group sizes in the Methods and abstract (51 females, 66 males) do not match the analysed counts (62 females, 51 males), the text contradicts itself on whether DI and NAIA males differ in body mass, and the pooled DI female jump height does not reconcile with the subgroup mean, so the source PDF should be checked before quoting these figures.
paper.practicalImplications: Because the DI-NAIA gap differed by sex in this sample, any CMJ benchmark for collegiate athletes should use separate male and female references rather than a pooled one. The values come from one force plate system and the flight-time method, so they may not transfer directly to other devices or methods.
paper.athleteDev: The group means can serve as a rough reference for similar collegiate groups tested with the same force plate and flight-time method, not as a standard for any individual athlete. The data do not show that a jump score predicts success at a competition level.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. Its athletes reported no injury in the six months before testing, it measured no return-to-play outcome, and its group averages cannot serve as a return-to-play benchmark for an individual.
